what: Phillips Edison owns shopping centres anchored by supermarkets. Its properties are neighbourhood centres in the United States where the main tenant is a grocery store and the surrounding units are let to pharmacies, restaurants, hairdressers, dentists and other businesses people visit regularly.
customers: Retail tenants: supermarket chains as anchors, and the local and national service businesses that want to be next to where people buy food every week.
money: Rent and tenant cost recoveries from about 300 grocery-anchored shopping centres.
moat: A supermarket draws people to the centre every week whether or not they intend to shop anywhere else, and that footfall is what the other tenants are paying for. Groceries are also the hardest retail category to move online at a profit, which makes this the most defensible type of physical retail property. Phillips Edison is one of the few landlords focused entirely on it.
risks: Free cash flow was about negative $177.1M, because a property company that is buying centres shows the purchases as cash outflows.
Debt of $2.4B against $3.5M of cash is normal for a property company but means refinancing risk whenever rates rise.
The shares trade at about 28.0 times earnings and 17.4 times EV/EBITDA, which is not cheap for a retail landlord.
Property earnings are depressed by depreciation that does not reflect economic wear, so the earnings multiple overstates the valuation — but it also means reported profit is a poor guide either way.
Thirteen analysts average a $43.46 target, only 8% above the current price.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year, from $532.8M in 2021 to $726.6M in 2025, through acquisitions and rent increases.
Grocery-anchored retail has the strongest occupancy and rent growth in physical retail, because food shopping resists online displacement.
The small-shop tenants around the anchor pay higher rents per square foot and renew at increases, which is where the growth comes from.
New construction of neighbourhood shopping centres has been almost nonexistent for fifteen years, so supply is effectively fixed.
watch: Occupancy and rent on renewal for the small-shop units, not the anchors. The supermarket pays low rent on a long lease; the shops around it are where the income grows or does not.
view: Grocery-anchored shopping centres are the one part of physical retail that survived the internet, and the reason is simple enough to state in a sentence: delivering food to someone’s door at a profit is extremely hard, and people keep driving to the supermarket every week. That weekly visit is the product Phillips Edison sells. The supermarket itself pays modest rent on a long lease and is not where the money is made; it is the reason a dentist, a nail salon, a sandwich shop and a pharmacy will pay well above that rate for the units around it.

So the number that describes this business is small-shop occupancy and small-shop renewal rent, and it is worth insisting on the distinction. Anchors are stable and low-yielding. The shops are where the rent grows, and they are also where the risk sits, because a local business fails more readily than a supermarket chain. Revenue has grown from $533 million to $727 million, which says both parts have been working.

The supply side is quietly important and gets little attention. Almost nobody has built a new neighbourhood shopping centre in the United States in fifteen years, because the economics never justified it once retail sentiment turned. That means the stock of these properties is effectively fixed while the population around them grows, and a landlord in a fixed-supply market with growing demand is in a good structural position.

The valuation is where I would push back. At 28 times earnings and 17.4 times EV/EBITDA, with thirteen analysts seeing 8% of upside, the market has fully noticed that this is the good kind of retail property. Property earnings are distorted by depreciation that bears no relation to economic wear, so the earnings multiple overstates the price somewhat — but the EV/EBITDA figure does not, and $2.4 billion of debt against almost no cash means every refinancing is a decision made by the bond market rather than by management. This is a high-quality portfolio at a price that assumes it stays high-quality.
bull: Fixed supply of neighbourhood centres meets growing population, small-shop rents renew upward on grocery footfall, and acquisitions keep compounding the portfolio.
bear: Small-shop tenants fail in a downturn while $2.4 billion of debt refinances at higher rates, and a 17 times EV/EBITDA multiple on a retail landlord contracts.
